notes.b: Congestion occurs when the volume of traffic on a road network exceeds the space and capacity available, so vehicles move slowly or stop. Most causes come from how cities grew and how people travel in them.
points: Rising car ownership puts more vehicles onto streets that were laid out for far fewer, so the same road space has to carry more traffic.

Low-density suburbs (spread-out housing with few homes per hectare) and commuter towns (towns whose residents travel to work elsewhere) are poorly served by public transport, so most journeys are made by car.
Radial roads (roads that run out from the centre like spokes) converge on a historic centre with narrow streets and few river crossings, funnelling traffic into one place.
Journeys to work and school peak at the same times of day, so the network is filled all at once.
Delivery vehicles and heavy goods vehicles (HGVs, large lorries) share the same streets as commuters and shoppers.
Jobs and shopping have dispersed (spread out) to suburbs that can be reached only by car, so even short trips add to road traffic.
Historically weak investment in rail has left cities without a fast alternative to the car.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level asks why a named city, such as Dublin, has high traffic congestion. Give several causes and tie each to the city.

notes.b: Congestion costs a city time, money and health. Several of its effects feed back into more congestion.
points: Workers lose time and productivity, and businesses face higher costs because deliveries and staff are delayed.
Commuters suffer stress and a reduced quality of life.
Stop-start traffic causes air and noise pollution, with carbon emissions from idling engines (engines left running while the vehicle is stationary).
Crowded routes lead to road accidents.
Buses are slowed by the same traffic, which makes public transport less attractive and so adds to car use.
Businesses and tourism are harmed by poor access to the centre.
There is less space for pedestrians and cyclists, because road space is given over to traffic.
notes.tip: A short question may ask for one problem of high car use. Pick one effect and say what it does, for example slower buses make people drive more.

notes.b: Dublin is the Irish city the exams use for traffic congestion. Its congestion comes from the way it spread out and the late arrival of alternatives to the car.
points: Sprawl (the spread of low-density development at the city edge) and car dependence bring large numbers of commuters into the city every day by car.
Radial routes converge on the centre, and there are few crossings of the River Liffey, so traffic is squeezed onto a handful of bridges.
The light rail network (electric trams) arrived late: the Luas opened in 2004, after the city's roads had already become congested.
Port traffic formerly ran through the city centre until the Port Tunnel opened in 2006.
notes.tip: If asked why Dublin has high traffic congestion, use these four reasons: sprawl and car dependence, radial routes with few Liffey crossings, late light rail, and port traffic through the centre.

notes.h: Traffic congestion: public transport and road measures
notes.b: Cities tackle congestion in two ways: by giving people a better alternative to the car and by managing where and how vehicles travel. These measures are mostly drawn from Dublin.
points: Public transport: DART (the electric commuter rail along the coast, opened 1984), Luas (opened 2004), commuter rail and BusConnects (a redesign of the bus network), plus the planned MetroLink, which has no date or cost yet.
Luas Cross City linked the Red and Green lines through the city centre in December 2017, so passengers could travel between the two lines.
Bus lanes and quality bus corridors give buses priority over cars, so buses are not slowed by general traffic.
Park and ride: car parks at the edge of the city where drivers can switch to public transport, so fewer cars enter the centre.
Cycle lanes and Dublin Bikes, the public bicycle scheme launched in 2009.
Integrated ticketing: the Leap card, introduced in 2011, allows one card to be used across different transport services.
Orbital roads and bypasses: the M50 orbital motorway, built in stages from 1990, takes traffic around the city instead of through it.
The Port Tunnel, opened in 2006, took port traffic out of the city centre; a 2007 restriction banned most five-axle heavy goods vehicles from the centre.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level asks for measures that can be taken, and for two examples of public transport. Give each measure as a separate point. Dublin's orbital road is the M50.

notes.h: Traffic congestion: reducing demand for car travel
notes.b: The second group of measures aims to cut the number of car journeys, by making driving dearer or by making journeys unnecessary.
points: Pedestrianisation: the busiest shopping streets are closed to traffic.
Parking charges and limits discourage commuters from driving into the centre.
Congestion charging: the London Congestion Charge, introduced in February 2003, is a daily charge to drive into central London on weekdays, and traffic in the zone fell in its early years.
Car sharing, remote working (working from home) and staggered working hours (different start times) spread traffic over time.
Land-use planning that puts homes close to jobs and transport reduces the need to travel by car.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level asks for two ways authorities reduce car use. Parking charges and the London Congestion Charge both fit. Do not give the London charge's price, as it changes.

notes.b: Urban decay is the physical, economic and social decline of part of a city, usually the inner city (the older area close to the centre). It is decline inside the built-up area, not growth at the edge.
points: Old industries and port jobs close, removing the economic base of the inner city.
Better-off residents move to the suburbs, leaving a smaller and poorer population behind.
Buildings are left derelict (empty and falling into disrepair) and are poorly maintained, particularly social housing (homes provided by the local authority).
Reduced rates income (the local tax paid by businesses and property) means the local authority has less money to maintain buildings and services.
Dereliction attracts crime and vandalism, which deter investment and residents.
Road schemes and planning blight: the threat of future road building leaves property uncertain, so owners stop investing in repairs.
notes.tip: Keep decay and sprawl apart. Decay is decline inside the city, usually the inner city; sprawl is uncontrolled growth at the edge, with different causes.

notes.b: Once decay begins, its effects reinforce each other, so a run-down area is hard to recover without outside help.
points: Unemployment and poverty among residents of the affected area, because local jobs have gone.
Derelict sites stand empty for long periods, because owners and investors see little reason to rebuild.
Population decline as families leave, so fewer people remain to support local shops and services.
Drug and crime problems, which grow where there are empty buildings and few jobs.
Poor services, because fewer people and less money remain to support them.
Stigma: the reputation of the area discourages investment and visitors.
A cycle of decline, in which each problem makes the others worse.

notes.h: Urban decay in Dublin's inner city
notes.b: Dublin's inner city shows how the loss of port jobs and the clearing of old housing left an area empty and run down.
points: Dublin's docks lost most of their jobs with containerisation (the shift to shipping goods in standard metal containers handled by machinery, needing far fewer workers) from the 1960s and 1970s.
Inner-city tenements (old, overcrowded rented housing) were cleared, and their residents moved to the suburbs.
Dereliction of inner-city streets and buildings followed through the 1970s and 1980s. There is more on this in Urban planning and renewal, which covers the renewal of these areas.

notes.b: Limerick is an Irish example of decay concentrated in social-housing estates rather than in the old centre.
points: Disadvantage (poverty and lack of opportunity) was concentrated in social-housing estates: Moyross, Southill, St Mary's Park and Ballinacurra Weston.
After an arson attack on two children in Moyross in 2006, the Government commissioned John Fitzgerald's report, published in 2007.
The report led to the Limerick Regeneration programme for Moyross, Southill, St Mary's Park and Ballinacurra Weston. There is more on its results in Urban planning and renewal.

notes.h: Urban decay in Detroit (developed-world case study)
notes.b: Detroit, Michigan, USA, is known as 'Motor City', the home of Ford, General Motors and Chrysler. Its decline shows decay on a city-wide scale.
points: Population peaked at about 1.85 million at the 1950 US census and fell to about 640,000 at the 2020 US census.
Middle-class, largely white families moved to the suburbs from the 1950s, helped by freeways (high-speed urban motorways), which left the city with fewer taxpayers.
Car-industry jobs moved out of the city or were automated (done by machines), so the city lost its main employer base.
Tens of thousands of houses were abandoned, because families had left and there was no demand for them.
Detroit filed for bankruptcy in July 2013, the largest municipal bankruptcy in US history, and exited it in December 2014.
Downtown and Midtown have since seen new investment, although many areas remain derelict.
notes.tip: Give only the checked figures: about 1.85 million in 1950 and about 640,000 in 2020. Do not add counts of vacant houses or debt totals.

notes.b: Urban sprawl is the uncontrolled outward spread of low-density housing and other development over rural land at the edge of a city. It is growth at the edge, unlike urban decay, which is decline inside the city.
points: Population growth, high prices in the inner city, and demand for houses with gardens push development outwards.
Car ownership and motorways make distant sites accessible, so people can live far from where they work.
Planning that zoned greenfield land (land never built on before) for development, and developers' preference for cheaper greenfield sites, drive building at the edge.
Tax incentives during the Celtic Tiger boom (the period of rapid Irish economic growth in the late 1990s and 2000s) encouraged building.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level asks you to name a city with sprawl, explain why it occurred and give one solution. Keep sprawl's causes separate from those of decay.

notes.b: Sprawl spreads people thinly over a large area, which is costly for the people who live there and for the city they left behind.
points: Long commutes and congestion, and car dependence, because distances are too long to walk or cycle and public transport is poor.
Loss of farmland and habitats, because rural land is built on. There is more on this in Urban land use and planning.
Costly services, such as roads, water and schools, spread thinly over a large area, so each household costs more to serve.
Dormitory towns, whose residents sleep there and work elsewhere, leaving little local activity.
Decline of the city centre as people and spending move out, and higher carbon emissions from longer car journeys.

notes.b: Dublin is the Irish example of sprawl, and its sprawl left a visible legacy when the property market collapsed.
points: Dublin's sprawl has extended into the commuter counties beyond the city boundary.
A Government survey in 2010 found almost 3,000 unfinished housing estates, known as ghost estates, after the 2008 property crash (the sudden collapse in house prices and building).

notes.b: Solutions either stop the city spreading outwards or make better use of land already built on.
points: Green belts: a protected ring of open land around the city to stop its spread.
Compact growth and brownfield development (reusing land that was built on before), set out in the National Planning Framework, to build on land within the city.
Higher densities of housing near public transport, so that fewer people need cars.
New towns planned as self-contained settlements with their own services, so residents do not have to travel far.
Regeneration of inner-city sites that are vacant or derelict, so growth is directed inwards.
notes.tip: Ireland has no statutory Dublin green belt, so do not claim one exists for Dublin. Compact growth and brownfield development are safer solutions to name.

notes.b: A community is a group of neighbours who know each other and share local life. In some urban areas the way housing was planned or built stops this from forming.
points: New estates are built quickly without schools, shops, community centres or public transport, so residents have nowhere to meet.
High-rise flats have no shared space where neighbours can meet.
Long commutes leave little time for local life.
Transient renting populations (tenants who move often) do not put down roots.
Old inner-city communities were demolished when tenements were cleared, breaking up established networks of family and neighbours.
Social segregation separates people by income and class into different areas.

notes.b: When a place has no shared life, the people in it feel the lack, and the area itself suffers.
points: Isolation and loneliness among residents who do not know their neighbours.
Anti-social behaviour, which is harder to deal with where neighbours do not know each other.
Little sense of belonging or local organisation, so there are few residents' groups or clubs to take action on local problems.

notes.h: Absence of community: examples and responses
notes.b: Examples come from Dublin and from Paris. The responses aim to build the facilities and involvement that were missing.
points: Ballymun's tower blocks in Dublin: seven 15-storey towers built 1966 to 1969, demolished 2004 to 2015.
Commuter estates and the ghost estates of Dublin's commuter counties.

Paris banlieues (the suburbs on the edge of Paris): large grands ensembles (estates built in the 1950s to 1970s) such as Sarcelles, with high unemployment and the riots that began in Clichy-sous-Bois in October 2005.
Responses: community facilities built alongside housing, with phasing conditions (planning rules) so that schools and shops come before the homes are occupied.
Responses: regeneration with resident participation, mixed tenure (a mix of owned, rented and social homes in one area), and sports clubs and family resource centres.

notes.b: Urban heritage includes historic buildings, streetscapes (the look of a street as a whole), archaeological sites and monuments, together with their setting. It is valuable in three ways.
points: Identity: heritage gives a city and its residents a sense of their history and place.
Tourism: historic buildings and monuments attract visitors and the income they bring.
Economic value: restored heritage buildings can support shops, hotels and cultural venues.
notes.tip: A short question may ask for one benefit of an urban heritage site. Give identity, tourism or economic value, with a reason.

notes.b: Heritage is easily lost because the pressures of a growing city work against old buildings.
points: Demolition for offices and roads, as when historic buildings are cleared for new development.
Neglect and dereliction of old buildings, so that without repair they decay and may have to be demolished.
Inappropriate new buildings, with heights that are out of scale with the historic streetscape.
Traffic vibration and pollution, which damage old buildings and monuments.
Tourist pressure, which can wear down historic sites and crowd out local residents.

notes.b: Dublin has both losses and successes. The losses show the threats above, and the reuse examples show heritage put to work.
points: Lower Fitzwilliam Street: the ESB (Ireland's electricity company) demolished a row of 16 Georgian houses in 1965 to build its head office. That office block has itself since been demolished and replaced.
Wood Quay: one of the largest Viking-age sites in Europe. Despite protests and court cases in the late 1970s, Dublin Corporation (the city council) built its civic offices on the site.
14 to 17 Moore Street, where the 1916 leaders spent their last hours before surrender, was declared a national monument in 2007.
Positive reuse: Temple Bar was regenerated in the 1990s, and Docklands warehouses have been reused for new purposes.
notes.tip: For Wood Quay, give no march size or date of a final court ruling; for Moore Street, no later court cases. Do not call any Dublin site a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

notes.b: Heritage is protected by law, by voluntary groups and by international listing.
points: The Planning and Development Act 2000 created the Record of Protected Structures (a list of buildings the law protects) and Architectural Conservation Areas (whole areas protected for their character).
National monuments are protected by the State.
An Taisce (the National Trust for Ireland), founded in 1948, campaigns for the protection of heritage.

UNESCO World Heritage listing (international recognition of sites of outstanding value): Ireland's two World Heritage Sites are Brú na Bóinne, listed in 1993, and Skellig Michael, listed in 1996. Neither is urban.
International urban examples: the Old and New Towns of Edinburgh, listed by UNESCO in 1995, and the Historic Centre of Rome, listed in 1980.

notes.h: Heritage tourism in a smaller Irish city
notes.b: Heritage attracts visitors in smaller cities as well as in Dublin.
points: Kilkenny's Medieval Mile attracts heritage tourism to a smaller Irish city. There is more on its medieval history in Pre-historic and historic settlement.

notes.b: Environmental quality is how clean, quiet and pleasant an urban area is. Air quality is the first aspect, and Dublin's ban on smoky coal is the Irish example of a response to air pollution.
points: Sources of urban air pollution: smoke from coal fires, and traffic emissions of nitrogen dioxide and particulates (tiny solid particles in the air).
Dublin's severe winter smog (smoke and fog mixed) in the 1980s led to the ban on smoky coal in Dublin from 1 September 1990.
Research after the ban found that black smoke levels and winter death rates fell.
The ban on smoky coal was extended nationwide in October 2022.
notes.tip: Do not give a number of lives saved by the coal ban.

notes.b: Cities produce large amounts of sewage and polluted runoff, which must be treated before it reaches rivers and the sea.
points: The Ringsend wastewater treatment plant treats most of Dublin's sewage and discharges into Dublin Bay.
The Ringsend plant is being upgraded, so that it can keep treating the sewage of a growing city.
Storm overflows: heavy rain can send mixed sewage and surface water into urban rivers and the bay, because the drains cannot carry the extra volume.
Urban rivers carry pollution from paved surfaces, roads and drains.

notes.b: Waste that is not recycled or treated becomes litter or goes to landfill, which harms the look and quality of an urban area. Ireland has used charges, recycling and energy recovery to cut it.
points: Litter and landfill: waste that is not recycled or treated goes to landfill (buried in the ground).
Plastic bag levy: introduced in March 2002 at 15 cent, after which plastic bag use fell sharply, showing a charge can change behaviour.
Recycling schemes reduce the amount of waste sent to landfill, because materials are reused instead of buried.
Poolbeg (Dublin Waste-to-Energy) incinerator, operating since 2017, burns residual waste (what is left after recycling) to generate energy.

notes.h: Environmental quality: noise, visual pollution and derelict land
notes.b: Not all pollution is chemical. Noise and an ugly environment also lower the quality of life in a city.
points: Noise from traffic, construction and night-time activity affects residents, for example by disturbing sleep.
Visual pollution: graffiti, poor signage and unsightly derelict buildings reduce the quality of the streetscape.
Derelict sites: the Derelict Sites levy is a charge on owners of derelict property to encourage its reuse.

notes.h: Environmental quality: green space and biodiversity
notes.b: Green space gives wildlife a home and gives residents somewhere to relax. Dublin has several examples.
points: Parks provide habitats and recreation: Phoenix Park, about 700 hectares, established 1662.
Canals provide green corridors (strips of greenery that wildlife can move along) through the city: the Royal Canal and the Grand Canal.
North Bull Island, in Dublin Bay, is a green space beside the city.
Loss of green space to infill: small gaps between buildings are built on, reducing open space for wildlife and residents.

notes.b: Building over land changes how water and heat behave in a city, which causes two problems.
points: Urban flooding: paved surfaces stop rain soaking into the ground, so runoff (water flowing over the surface) rises quickly into rivers and drains.
Hurricane Charley, in August 1986, caused severe flooding of the River Dodder in Dublin.
Urban heat island: built-up areas are warmer than the surrounding countryside because buildings and paving absorb and hold heat.

keyTerms.definition: A condition in which traffic volume exceeds the capacity of the road network, so vehicles move slowly or stop.
A road that runs from the outskirts of a city towards its centre, funnelling traffic into one place.
Car parks at the edge of a city where drivers leave their cars and continue by public transport.
A daily charge for driving into a designated central area, used to reduce traffic.
The physical, economic and social decline of part of a city, usually the inner city.
Describes an abandoned building or site that has fallen into disrepair and is no longer used.
The uncontrolled outward spread of low-density development over rural land at the edge of a city.
An unfinished or largely empty housing estate, left after a property development stalls.
A town whose residents mainly sleep there and commute to work elsewhere, leaving little local activity.
The lack of local facilities, networks and sense of belonging in a new or isolated residential area.
A list, kept by each local authority under the Planning and Development Act 2000, of buildings to be protected.
An area of special architectural or historic character, protected under the Planning and Development Act 2000.
An outlet that releases mixed sewage and surface water into rivers or the sea when heavy rain overloads a sewage system.
The effect by which built-up areas are warmer than the surrounding countryside.

factCards.term: Traffic congestion in cities: causes
factCards.definition: More cars; low-density suburbs poorly served by public transport; radial roads into a historic centre with narrow streets and few river crossings; work and school trips at one peak; delivery lorries; car-only suburban jobs and shops; weak rail investment.

factCards.term: Traffic congestion in cities: effects
factCards.definition: Lost time and productivity; stress; air and noise pollution and carbon emissions; road accidents; slower buses, which pushes more people into cars; businesses and tourism harmed; less space for pedestrians and cyclists.

factCards.term: Why Dublin has high traffic congestion: four reasons
factCards.definition: Sprawl and car dependence bring commuters in by car; radial routes converge on the centre and there are few Liffey crossings; light rail arrived late (Luas, 2004); port traffic ran through the city centre until the Port Tunnel opened in 2006.

factCards.term: Dublin public transport measures with dates
factCards.definition: DART, 1984; Luas, 2004, with Luas Cross City linking the Red and Green lines in December 2017; Dublin Bikes, 2009; Leap card integrated ticketing, 2011; BusConnects redesigning the bus network; MetroLink planned.

factCards.term: Road, freight and demand measures to cut congestion in Dublin
factCards.definition: M50 orbital motorway, built in stages from 1990; Port Tunnel, 2006, then a 2007 ban on most five-axle heavy goods vehicles in the centre; bus lanes and quality bus corridors; park and ride; pedestrianisation; parking charges; remote working.

factCards.term: London: two charges used to cut traffic and emissions
factCards.definition: The Congestion Charge, from February 2003, a daily charge to drive into central London on weekdays; traffic in the zone fell in its early years. The Ultra Low Emission Zone, from 2019, extended London-wide in August 2023.

factCards.term: Urban decay: causes
factCards.definition: Old industries and port jobs close; better-off residents move to the suburbs; buildings, especially social housing, are left derelict or poorly maintained; reduced rates income; dereliction attracts crime and vandalism; road schemes cause planning blight.

factCards.term: Urban decay: effects
factCards.definition: Unemployment and poverty; derelict sites standing empty for years; population decline; drug and crime problems; poor services; stigma that deters investment and visitors; a cycle of decline in which each problem worsens the others.

factCards.term: Dublin's inner city in the 1970s and 1980s: how it decayed
factCards.definition: The docks lost most of their jobs with containerisation from the 1960s and 1970s; inner-city tenements were cleared and residents moved to the suburbs; dereliction of streets and buildings followed.

factCards.term: Limerick: decay in social-housing estates and the response
factCards.definition: Concentrated disadvantage in Moyross, Southill, St Mary's Park and Ballinacurra Weston. After an arson attack on two children in Moyross in 2006, John Fitzgerald's 2007 report led to the Limerick Regeneration programme.

factCards.term: Detroit: why the city decayed
factCards.definition: Known as Motor City, home of Ford, General Motors and Chrysler. Middle-class, largely white families moved to the suburbs from the 1950s, helped by freeways; car-industry jobs moved out or were automated; tens of thousands of houses were abandoned.

factCards.term: Detroit: population figures, bankruptcy and recovery
factCards.definition: Population peaked at about 1.85 million (1950 US census) and fell to about 640,000 (2020). Filed for bankruptcy in July 2013, the largest municipal bankruptcy in US history, and exited in December 2014. Downtown and Midtown have since seen new investment.

factCards.term: Urban sprawl: causes and effects
factCards.definition: Causes: population growth, high inner-city prices, demand for gardens, cars and motorways, greenfield zoning, Celtic Tiger tax incentives. Effects: long commutes, car dependence, lost farmland, thinly spread services, dormitory towns, city-centre decline.

factCards.term: Dublin's sprawl: where it spread and the ghost estates
factCards.definition: Into the commuter counties, to towns such as Navan, Ashbourne, Naas, Newbridge, Maynooth, Bray and Greystones. A Government survey in 2010 found almost 3,000 unfinished housing estates (ghost estates) after the 2008 property crash.

factCards.term: Urban sprawl: five solutions
factCards.definition: Green belts; compact growth and brownfield development under the National Planning Framework; higher housing densities near public transport; new towns with their own services; regeneration of vacant or derelict inner-city sites.

factCards.term: Absence of community: causes
factCards.definition: Estates built quickly without schools, shops, community centres or public transport; high-rise flats with no shared space; long commutes; transient renting populations; old inner-city communities broken up by tenement clearance; social segregation.

factCards.term: Absence of community: three examples
factCards.definition: Ballymun, Dublin: seven 15-storey towers built 1966–69, demolished 2004–2015. Commuter and ghost estates in Dublin's commuter counties. Paris banlieues: grands ensembles such as Sarcelles, high unemployment, and riots from Clichy-sous-Bois in October 2005.

factCards.term: Absence of community: effects and responses
factCards.definition: Effects: isolation, loneliness, anti-social behaviour, little sense of belonging. Responses: community facilities built with housing (phasing conditions); regeneration with resident participation; mixed tenure; sports clubs and family resource centres.

factCards.term: Urban heritage: three benefits and five threats
factCards.definition: Value: a sense of identity; tourism income; economic reuse for shops, hotels and venues. Threats: demolition for offices and roads; neglect and dereliction; out-of-scale new buildings; traffic vibration and pollution; tourist pressure.

factCards.term: Dublin heritage losses: Fitzwilliam Street and Wood Quay
factCards.definition: Lower Fitzwilliam Street: the ESB demolished a row of 16 Georgian houses in 1965 for its head office. Wood Quay, one of Europe's largest Viking-age sites: despite protests and court cases in the late 1970s, Dublin Corporation built its civic offices there.

factCards.term: Dublin heritage: Moore Street and two cases of positive reuse
factCards.definition: 14–17 Moore Street, where the 1916 leaders spent their last hours before surrender, was declared a national monument in 2007. Positive reuse: Temple Bar regenerated as a cultural quarter in the 1990s; Docklands warehouses reused.

factCards.term: Urban heritage protection: four methods with examples
factCards.definition: Record of Protected Structures and Architectural Conservation Areas (Planning and Development Act 2000); national monuments; An Taisce, founded 1948; UNESCO listing, e.g. Edinburgh's Old and New Towns (1995) and Rome's Historic Centre (1980).

factCards.term: Dublin's smoky coal ban: dates and results
factCards.definition: Smoky coal was banned in Dublin from 1 September 1990 after severe winter smog in the 1980s; black smoke levels and winter death rates fell afterwards. The ban was extended nationwide in October 2022.

factCards.term: Water and waste in Dublin: three named responses
factCards.definition: Ringsend wastewater treatment plant treats most of Dublin's sewage, discharging into Dublin Bay, and is being upgraded; the plastic bag levy, March 2002, at 15 cent, cut bag use sharply; the Poolbeg waste-to-energy incinerator has operated since 2017.

factCards.term: Urban green space and flooding: Dublin examples
factCards.definition: Phoenix Park (about 700 hectares, 1662), the Royal and Grand Canals and North Bull Island give green space, but small gaps are lost to infill. Paved surfaces speed runoff into rivers and drains; rivers also flood, as when Hurricane Charley, August 1986, caused severe flooding of the River Dodder.

questions.prompt: Discuss two of the following issues that may arise from the growth of urban settlements: heritage issues; environmental issues.
questions.model: Heritage issues: 1. Urban heritage includes historic buildings, streetscapes, archaeological sites and monuments, which give a city its identity, attract tourists and support the economy. 2. Threats include demolition for offices and roads, neglect and dereliction, and inappropriate new buildings out of scale with the historic streetscape. 3. Traffic vibration and pollution damage old buildings, and tourist pressure can wear down sites. 4. Dublin: the ESB demolished 16 Georgian houses on Lower Fitzwilliam Street in 1965 to build its head office. 5. Dublin: Wood Quay, one of the largest Viking-age sites in Europe, was built over by Dublin Corporation's civic offices despite protests and court cases in the late 1970s. 6. Dublin: 14 to 17 Moore Street, where the 1916 leaders spent their last hours before surrender, was declared a national monument in 2007. 7. Protection: the Planning and Development Act 2000 created the Record of Protected Structures and Architectural Conservation Areas, and An Taisce, founded in 1948, campaigns for heritage. Environmental issues: 8. Air: smoke from coal fires and traffic emissions of nitrogen dioxide and particulates. 9. Dublin's severe winter smog in the 1980s led to the smoky coal ban from 1 September 1990; black smoke levels and winter death rates fell afterwards. 10. Water: the Ringsend plant treats most of Dublin's sewage and discharges into Dublin Bay, and storm overflows send mixed sewage into rivers. 11. Waste: the plastic bag levy of March 2002 cut plastic bag use sharply, and the Poolbeg incinerator has operated since 2017. 12. Visual and noise pollution, graffiti and derelict sites, which the Derelict Sites levy aims to address. 13. Green space is lost to infill, while Phoenix Park, about 700 hectares, established 1662, provides habitat and recreation. 14. Urban flooding from paved surfaces, as in the River Dodder flooding of August 1986, and the urban heat island effect. Conclusion: both heritage and environmental problems follow from growth, and the planning response to them is evaluated in the note Urban planning and renewal.

questions.prompt: Discuss three of the following urban problems with reference to examples you have studied: traffic congestion, urban decay, urban sprawl.
questions.model: Traffic congestion (Dublin): 1. Radial roads converge on the centre, with few crossings of the Liffey, and car dependence brings commuters in daily. 2. Effects include lost time, stress, pollution and slower buses. 3. Measures include DART, the Luas (2004), BusConnects, bus lanes, the M50 and the Port Tunnel (2006), with the 2007 HGV restriction. 4. Dublin Bikes (2009) and the Leap card (2011) support cycling and integrated travel. 5. The London Congestion Charge (February 2003) shows how a charge can cut traffic in a central area. Urban decay (Detroit): 1. Population fell from about 1.85 million in 1950 to about 640,000 in 2020. 2. Middle-class families moved to the suburbs from the 1950s, helped by freeways. 3. Car-industry jobs moved out or were automated, and tens of thousands of houses were abandoned. 4. Detroit filed for bankruptcy in July 2013, the largest municipal bankruptcy in US history. 5. Downtown and Midtown now have new investment, but many areas remain derelict. Urban sprawl (Dublin): 1. Causes include population growth, high inner-city prices, demand for gardens, car ownership and motorways, and planning that zoned greenfield land. 2. Effects include long commutes, loss of farmland and habitats, costly services spread thinly, and dormitory towns. 3. Sprawl extended into the commuter counties, and a 2010 survey found almost 3,000 ghost estates after the 2008 crash. 4. Solutions include green belts, compact growth and brownfield development under the National Planning Framework, and higher densities near public transport. Conclusion: each problem has different causes, with decay inside the city and sprawl at its edge.

questions.prompt: (i) Name one city where urban sprawl has occurred. (ii) Explain why. (iii) Describe one solution.
questions.model: (i) Dublin. (ii) Causes: population growth and high prices in the inner city led households to seek houses with gardens on the edge, where planning had zoned greenfield land for development. Car ownership and motorways made distant sites reachable, and developers preferred cheaper greenfield sites. Tax incentives during the Celtic Tiger boom encouraged building further out. The result was sprawl into the commuter counties, with long commutes and loss of farmland. (iii) Solution: compact growth on brownfield land near public transport. Vacant and derelict urban sites are redeveloped at higher density, so fewer people need cars and less farmland is lost. This is set out in the National Planning Framework, which aims for 40% of new homes to be within the built-up footprint of existing settlements.
